Reflection on 4th July E-commerce Event – Expanded

On 4th July, I had the pleasure of joining fellow ecommerce brands for a fantastic merchants’ dinner in London at the Coal office. 

During the evening, I gave a short talk about what we’re doing at Rusty Monkey, including our current offering and some co-marketing ideas. It was a brilliant opportunity to share our work, and it sparked some great conversations with other brands about future collaborations.

The event brought together a wide mix of people from across the e-commerce world including platforms, agencies, marketplaces, and retailers. It was inspiring to connect with such a knowledgeable group and hear how others are approaching shared challenges and opportunities in the industry.

Marketing insights and strategies:

Much of the evening centred around relationship building and collaboration. We discussed different approaches to co-marketing, how to create value-led partnerships, and how to better track marketing performance across multiple channels. I came away with fresh ideas on using data to personalise customer experiences and how to better align marketing activity with business goals particularly in a fastchanging ecommerce environment.

How does this connect to my role?

This experience really ties in with my current responsibilities at Rusty Monkey. I'm actively involved in developing our marketing strategy and supporting client engagement, so the conversations I had and the insights I gained were directly relevant. Presenting at the event helped build my confidence in talking about our brand and services, and the potential collaborations we discussed may lead to new opportunities that I’ll help drive forward.

Knowledge, Skills and Behaviours (KSBs) developed:

Knowledge: I strengthened my understanding of marketing techniques, co-marketing strategies, and current trends in ecommerce (K1, K5).

Skills: I developed my presentation and communication skills, especially in a professional networking context. I also built new working relationships that could lead to joint projects (S3, S5, S6).

Behaviours: I showed initiative and professionalism by representing the company, and I demonstrated a strong commitment to ongoing learning and development (B1, B3).

I'm genuinely excited about what could come from this event, both in terms of new connections and how it supports my own growth in the role.

Today, I co-facilitated a dynamic and forward-thinking session titled “Early Careers Recruitment Marketing 2026 Planning Workshop”, alongside our Employer Brand Manager. The workshop aimed to identify key challenges and opportunities in recruitment marketing, laying the groundwork for a strategic plan that supports the Early Careers team’s ambitious goal: a 40% increase in high-quality applications from diverse talent pools.

This initiative directly connects to several core marketing principles, including K1.1 Marketing theory (segmentation, branding, product lifecycle), K1.2 Brand & reputation (brand positioning, tone of voice), and K2.2 Marketing’s business impact, as we explored how marketing can drive measurable outcomes for talent acquisition.

As the Creative Services Executive, I proposed a multi-channel strategy that blends digital innovation with direct engagement. This included:

Digital marketing tactics:
- Social media campaigns tailored to early-career audiences (K4.3 Communication channels, S1.1 Channel coordination)
- Optimised website content and landing pages for conversion (K2.3 Customer decision-making, S1.3 Material production)
- Interactive webinars showcasing career paths and company culture (K3.1 Market research, S2.1 Communication)
- PPC and targeted Google Ads to reach niche talent pools (K4.2 Routes to market)
- YouTube content featuring employee stories and day-in-the-life videos (K1.2 Brand & reputation, S1.3 Material production)

Direct marketing initiatives:
- In-person career events and university fairs (K2.1 Business & sector context, S2.2 Stakeholder collaboration)
- Partnerships with student societies and STEM networks to build inclusive pipelines (K2.4 Legal & compliance, B4.3 Ethics & inclusion)
- Employer presentations and workshops to build brand awareness and trust (K1.3 Stakeholder & CRM, S2.1 Communication)

To ensure our campaigns are both effective and accountable, I will lead the evaluation process using analytics tools (S5.1 Campaign evaluation, S6.2 Digital tools) and interpret performance data to generate actionable insights (S5.2 Data analysis, S5.3 Insight generation). Key metrics will include:
- Application volume and quality
- Webinar and event registrations
- Social media engagement
- Website traffic and conversion rates

This approach reflects a strong understanding of K2.3 Customer decision-making and K3.1 Market research, ensuring our strategy is audience-centric and evidence-based. Throughout the session, I demonstrated B2.1 Creativity and B2.2 Solution thinking by proposing fresh ideas and practical improvements, while maintaining B1.1 Drive & completion and B4.2 Collaboration in a cross-functional setting.

Today, I facilitated a recruitment marketing strategy session, and here is a summary.

1. Employer Branding & Recruitment Marketing
Plan: Develop a structured employer brand and recruitment marketing plan for 2026 with quarterly activities (K1.1 Marketing theory, K1.2 Brand & reputation, S1.2 Campaign planning, S1.1 Channel coordination, and B1.1 Drive & completion).
EVP: Create a clear Employee Value Proposition (EVP) and embed it in social media, job adverts, and the careers website (K1.2 Brand & reputation, S1.3 Material production, and B2.1 Creativity – generating fresh ideas for authentic and engaging content).
Toolkits: Provide templates for hiring posts to ensure consistent messaging (S1.3 Material production and S2.1 Communication).
Career Site: Enhance it with authentic employee testimonials and visuals (K1.2 Brand & reputation, S1.3 Material production, and B2.1 Creativity).

2. Salary & Compensation Challenges
Issue: Salary competitiveness is a major barrier for electricians, engineers, and supervisors (K2.1 Business & sector context and K2.2 Marketing’s business impact).
Transparency and brand awareness: Lack of clear salary bands complicates advertising (K2.4 Legal & compliance and B4.3 Ethics & inclusion – promoting fairness and transparency in job adverts).
Align pay with market standards (K2.2 Marketing’s business impact and B2.2 Solution thinking – proposing practical improvements to pay structures).

3. Diversity and Inclusion
Goal: Increase diversity, especially among women and ethnic minorities, in senior roles (K2.4 Legal & compliance and B4.3 Ethics & inclusion).
Showcase employee resource groups: Promote these and foster an inclusive culture (K1.2 Brand & reputation, S2.2 Stakeholder collaboration, and B4.2 Collaboration).
Conversion: Address the low progression of ethnic minorities into senior roles (K3.1 Market research and S5.3 Insight generation).

4. Brand Recognition & Candidate Experience
Confusion exists between WPS and the parent company branding (K1.2 Brand & reputation and S2.1 Communication).
Solution: Improve the career site and LinkedIn presence to enhance candidate experience (S1.1 Channel coordination and B1.2 Adaptability).

5. Recruitment Channels & Strategies
Current reliance: CV Library and LinkedIn (K4.3 Communication channels).
Future initiatives: Explore AI-driven tools, attend housing conferences, and leverage referral schemes (K4.2 Routes to market, S1.2 Campaign planning, and B1.2 Adaptability).
Content: Share authentic employee stories and day-in-the-life content (K1.2 Brand & reputation, S1.3 Material production, and B2.1 Creativity).

6. Measurement & Next Steps
KPIs: Establish measurable targets, such as application numbers and social media metrics (S5.1 Campaign evaluation and S5.2 Data analysis).
Tools: Utilise ATS and analytics to track progress (S6.2 Digital tools and B3.1 Learning mindset).
Action items: Clarify job advertising within the organisation's property division, gather diversity data, and draft a prioritised plan (S3.1 Time & project management and B1.1 Drive & completion).

Following the lecture on secondary data, I recognised that knowledge of wider industry trends and competitor activity was something lacking in our monthly marketing performance reviews.
In a meeting with my line manager (the Marketing Manager) I suggested the idea for doing a trends/competitor update in our monthly meeting so that we can be aware of any threats or opportunities for our marketing. 

I prepared for the meeting by doing some research on what information I could use, including reports such as Statista, Mintel etc. and who our main competitiors are. I outlined the case and my Line Manager agreed that this was a great idea.

By recommending this idea, I have demonstrated a proactive approach and initiative to improve our marketing processes (B1), evidence of communication (S2), creative thinking & commitment to continous improvement so we can utilise evidence for insightful recommendations (B2), evaluation and analysis by doing initial research that will drive marketing insights (S5) and awareness of different products and distribution channels by reviewing our competitors and what they offer (K3).

Watching Art & Copy gave me insight into how creativity and strategy combine to create iconic campaigns (B2.1, B2.2, K1.1). I attended the CMO’s Guide to Growth 2026 event, which focused on turning performance marketing into long‑term sustainable growth by using seven strategic levers (K2.2). It was interesting to hear expert speakers discuss how brand discovery is changing, how to connect with customers across fragmented journeys, and how measurement and experimentation can unlock better outcomes (K1.1, K2.3) .

One valuable takeaway was the emphasis on setting up robust measurement frameworks and analytics that support smarter decisions and growth, reinforcing the importance of data quality, tracking, and insight generation (S5.2, S5.3, S6.2) . The session on experimentation in particular encouraged moving beyond assumptions and using structured test‑and‑learn approaches (S5.3), which aligns with ideas from our course about avoiding bias and making decisions grounded in evidence.

I also appreciated the discussions around balancing performance with broader brand building and community engagement, highlighting how integrated thinking and strategic oversight are vital in modern marketing (K1.2, S2.2) .

Overall, attending this event helped reinforce that combining data, experimentation, and strategic insight is crucial for effective marketing that drives both short‑ and long‑term goals.

Attended AMA webinar: Using AI with judgement

Session covered environmental impacts, developing AI models using the Latent Space Game, practical examples using Theory Machine mechanics, and the 4D AI fluency framework. Also group discussion on when AI-generated imagery should or should not be approved in individual organisations.

General consensus was that fully AI generated images would not be approved, with discussion around accuracy and the impact on illustrators/artists. In terms on editing, some AI image editing could be approved dependent on context, but in most cases non-AI options (e.g. cropping the offending area out of the image manually) would give similar or better effects. All agreed that generating backgrounds which do not exist, or removing key identifying aspects of a venue space were not acceptable and would not be approved.

Facebook Boost and Ad Campaign for School Open Days

To promote awareness of our Trust schools’ open days, I trialled two approaches on Facebook to assess engagement and reach:

Initial Facebook Post Boost
The first attempt was a Facebook boost of a post for 7 days. This helped increase organic reach slightly and gave a baseline for audience engagement. Metrics from this boost were reviewed to inform the next step.

Facebook Ad Campaign
Following the boost, I ran a Facebook advert for 7 days with a total spend of £41.98. The ad included a short video promoting the school open days.

Ad Performance Metrics:
Total views: 5,202
Unique viewers: 3,474
Link clicks: 132
Post engagements (likes, comments, shares, reactions): 1,981
3-second video plays: 1,837

Audience Insights:
Devices:
Viewed on mobile: 2,036
Facebook mobile app feeds: 1,091
Facebook Reels: 327

Demographics:
Largest audience: 35–44 year-old females
Other significant age groups: 25–34, 45–54, 55–64
This indicated that the ad reached parents and family members effectively.

Summary / Analysis:
The Facebook ad outperformed the initial post boost in terms of engagement, reach, and interaction. It successfully generated meaningful engagement with local families, leading to a substantial number of tour bookings across the schools. The use of a short, visually engaging video optimized for mobile devices proved particularly effective.

Reflection / Next Steps:
Short, mobile-optimised videos are more effective than standard post boosts for engagement and link clicks.
Testing different creative approaches (images, messaging, or video content) could further increase click-through and booking rates.
Content from the ad can be repurposed for organic posts across school and Trust pages to maintain visibility and momentum.

Following our recent Trust Parent Voice Survey, results have been analysed and the outcomes are detailed below, which leads me to attach the following document to serve as a useful prompt for communications.

Following a recent marketing meeting with the Headteacher at Selling CE Primary School, I became aware of an underutilised space within the school building that includes a room with access to a garden area, a kitchen space, and a smaller breakout area. This presented an immediate opportunity to explore how the space could be used more effectively to strengthen parental engagement and community links.

I identified this as a valuable resource that could support a wider programme of parent-focused activity, such as stay-and-play sessions, workshops, and community learning opportunities. As a result, I contacted the local Adult Education Centre, who expressed strong interest in working with the school. A follow-up meeting has now been arranged to explore potential course offerings, including practical sessions such as healthy air fryer cooking, budget-friendly meal planning, CV writing, volunteering pathways, Teaching Assistant taster sessions, first aid training, and workshops supporting parents with issues such as children’s sleep routines.

To ensure this offer is shaped by parental need and interest, I have developed a short Microsoft Forms survey to gather initial feedback from parents and carers. This will help inform the direction and relevance of the proposed sessions. In addition, I plan to undertake further engagement activity a week after distribution by speaking directly with parents at pick-up time, using a QR code to capture additional responses and increase participation from those who may not have completed the online survey. This blended approach will help ensure a broader and more representative understanding of parental views.

Ultimately, this work aims to strengthen relationships between families and the school by creating meaningful opportunities for engagement, learning, and connection. By offering relevant and accessible sessions for parents, we hope to enhance their sense of belonging and satisfaction within the school community, encouraging them to share positive experiences with friends, family, and the wider community. In turn, this increased advocacy and community engagement has the potential to support future pupil recruitment and help ensure continued growth in admissions.

Reflections from Internal Management Meeting

Attending an internal management meeting gave me a clearer picture of both operational priorities and marketing alignment. Here is what I learned and how it connects to my marketing role at Exporter Services:

1. CRM Misalignment and System Knowledge
I discovered that HubSpot, which I had already begun to use, is not compatible with our systems (specifically Outlook), and that the business is actually moving forward with MailChimp. This highlighted a gap in internal communication and the importance of stakeholder alignment. It links directly to K1.3 (internal CRM/stakeholder coordination), S6.2 (using appropriate systems), and B3.1, as I recognised the mistake and adjusted course accordingly.

2. Consistent Contact Information on Promotional Materials
I learned that all marketing materials should use team@exporter-services instead of training@ to ensure inquiries are picked up efficiently. This reminded me how small operational details can impact campaign success, and reinforced the importance of internal communication. It relates to S3.3 (managing internal stakeholders), K1.3, and B4.2 (collaborative working).

3. Strategic Focus: Promote What Needs Growth
The business has recently gained seven new contracts, meaning operations are close to capacity. However, private training bookings are low. This helped me realise I should shift focus from promoting operations to raising awareness about our training offer. This shows how marketing must flex with business priorities (K2.2) and tailor its activities to business needs (S1.2, S5.2).

4. Business Turnover and Course Volumes
The company didn't meet its £1m turnover target last year and is aiming to hit it this year. I also learned that Chambers-led courses are down, but there’s renewed interest following James' conversations with them. This informs how I prioritise marketing effort and measure impact, linking to K2.1, S1.1, and S5.1 (evaluating effectiveness).

5. Upholding Value Over Discounting
There was agreement that lowering prices to win business isn't the right approach. Instead, we need to better communicate the value of training - particularly for compliance and cost-saving benefits. I support this fully and plan to focus messaging accordingly. This supports K1.2 (brand and reputation), S2.1 (producing persuasive communication), and B4.3 (ethical practice).

6. SEO Success and Blog Strategy
We’ve had a rise in organic website traffic, with people finding us through key terms like “Incoterms” and “commodity codes.” I volunteered to write a weekly blog to support this momentum. I plan to use tools like AnswerThePublic to guide topics, which aligns with K3.1 (market research), S5.3 (deriving insights), and B1.2/B2.1 (self-starting and creative problem solving).

Reading chapter 7

This chapter helped me understand that marketing is not just about promoting a product - it’s about understanding who the customer is, why they make decisions, and how we can meet their needs better than competitors.

One of the key concepts I took from this reading was the STP model: Segmenting, Targeting, and Positioning. I used this framework to refine our social media approach. I realised that trying to speak to “everyone” leads to vague, ineffective messages. By creating defined customer personas, I could craft LinkedIn posts that spoke directly to the challenges, motivations, and language of different audience types. This made our content more relevant and human.

Another takeaway was the importance of buyer behaviour. I hadn’t thought as deeply before about how decisions are influenced by emotional, psychological, social, and personal factors. For example, understanding that one of our personas is motivated by compliance pressure and risk reduction changed how I wrote for them — I focused more on clarity, authority, and reassurance.

The section on decision-making stages (K2.3) also helped me think more strategically. I started mapping our content to different points in the buyer journey, for example, using a LinkedIn post to create awareness of a problem, and then linking to a blog post that helps the reader evaluate their options. That shift made my writing more purposeful.

Lastly, the concept of personas as real tools, not just theoretical exercises, really stuck with me. I used insights from our existing clients and what I know about their behaviour to build three personas. This not only gave me more confidence in my writing, but it helped me link the theory to real marketing outputs. It also supported my understanding of K1.1, K3.1, and S5.2.

Reflective Summary – 1:1 with Crispin Reed
Date: 27/06/25

What I Did / Learnt

In my 1:1 with Crispin Reed, we discussed strategies for reaching new leads for our training services. I shared my idea of contacting 10 prospects via email using Outlook. He advised making the emails highly personalised, linking the message to something the recipient has posted online or is interested in. Although I sent the emails, I haven’t heard back yet and haven’t followed up with a call (as planned).

Crispin suggested:

- Trialling cold outreach using a personalised pilot of 10 people
- Considering a bought lead list (e.g. PerlFinder in Manchester)
- Exploring trade magazine advertising, free webinars, and interviewing known names as hooks
- Asking current clients how they’d prefer to be approached and what would make us stand out

This session helped me think more tactically and customer-centrically, particularly about message relevance, timing, and channel choice.

Link to Knowledge, Skills, and Behaviours

K1.1 – Segmentation theory: We discussed targeting specific audience types (e.g. SME decision-makers in certain sectors). This reinforced the idea that outreach should be tailored to segmented audiences with specific needs.

K2.3 – Decision-making process: Crispin’s advice about researching what individuals post online shows how important it is to understand what drives buyer decisions – whether through emotional appeal, relevance, or social proof.

K3.1 and S5.2 – Market research and customer insight: The suggestion to ask existing clients how they want to be approached reflects using primary research to better understand buyer behaviour and improve future outreach.

B4.1 – Customer passion and professionalism: I was encouraged to think like the customer – to take the time to make outreach meaningful rather than generic, which shows respect and understanding of their role and interests.

Next Steps / Reflection

I plan to follow up the initial emails with a polite phone call, and I may also A/B test different email styles to improve engagement. I’ll also reach out to a few existing clients for feedback on how we can better market to them.

This session has helped me be more strategic and empathetic in my approach, and I now better understand how customer insight should guide all marketing actions.

Delegate Info Spreadsheet

To support our training activity at Exporter Services, I created a structured Excel spreadsheet to log delegate information. I’ve started entering real data from the last two courses, including each delegate’s name, job role, company, industry, course attended, and their reason for attending.

I built this tool to help me better understand our customers — particularly the types of people attending each course, what their job involves, and what problems they’re trying to solve. Once the LinkedIn integration with Mailchimp was activated, we ensured that every lead would be automatically tagged “Black Friday 2025” in our Mailchimp Audience. Activity: Diagnosing and Resolving a WooCommerce-Mailchimp Automation Failure

A customer purchased two on-demand video training courses via the Exporter Services website. The purchase was expected to trigger automated email sequences in Mailchimp, but no emails were sent. I investigated the issue end-to-end and implemented a permanent fix.

I began by reviewing the order details in WooCommerce and cross-referencing the Mailchimp automations dashboard, identifying that all four course email sequences were showing zero starts despite being active. I diagnosed that the automation trigger was tag-based ("Contact tagged"), but no tags were being applied to contacts on purchase. I then investigated the Mailchimp for WooCommerce plugin settings and established that while the plugin was connected and syncing correctly, it only supported blanket tagging of all contacts rather than product-specific tagging — meaning it could not apply different tags based on which course was purchased.

I explored several potential solutions methodically, including Zapier and webhook-based approaches, before identifying that the most appropriate solution was already available within our existing Mailchimp Standard plan: the "Buys a specific product" purchase trigger under Shopping Activity automations. I updated all four course automations by pausing each one, replacing the tag-based trigger with a product purchase trigger linked to the relevant course, and reactivating them. I also resolved the immediate customer issue by manually applying tags to the customer's contact record to ensure their sequences started without delay.

Additional Activity - Reading - Start With Why by Simon Sinek (Chapter Two)

In Chapter Two, Sinek highlights the use of manipulation in modern business and marketing. While often viewed negatively, many common tactics e.g. pricing discounts, promotions, fear appeals, aspirational messaging, peer pressure, and novelty - are forms of manipulation.

Pricing strategies like 'Buy-One-Get-One-Free' or charm pricing are discussed, as well as emotional triggers like fear or social proof. Sinek warns that these methods, though effective in driving short-term results, can foster dependency and undermine long-term customer loyalty and profitability.

Sinek likens them to a temporary fix, not a sustainable strategy. The key takeaway is that ethical, purpose-driven marketing offers a more enduring path - one that builds trust and loyalty rather than relying on repeated psychological triggers.

Additional Activity - Reading - Start With Why by Simon Sinek (Chapter Three)

Simon Sinek talks about the concept of 'The Golden Circle', and reveals how inspiring leaders and organisations communicate. Rather than manipulating behaviour, they ignite belief — and it all begins from the inside out, starting with WHY.

What – Every organisation knows what they do. These are the products/services they offer
How – Some know how they do it. This is often their unique process, value proposition, or differentiator
Why – Very few know why they do it. Why does the organisation exist? Why should anyone care?

Most companies communicate from the outside in — starting with what they do. But the most inspiring ones begin with why. They think, act, and speak from the inside out. Their purpose drives everything. They challenge the status quo and lead with belief. E.g. Apple don’t just sell technology — they sell a lifestyle, an experience. Every product reflects their core belief: to challenge convention and empower creativity. Their “why” is clear, and it resonates.

We all see the world through a personal lens. Brands that align with our worldview inspire loyalty. But when their “why” becomes unclear, that connection fades. Inspiration gives way to manipulation.

KSBs

Additional Activity - Reading - Start With Why by Simon Sinek (Chapter Four)

Simon Sinek links his concept of the Golden Circle to human biology, illustrating how it mirrors the way our brains function. The limbic brain—which corresponds to the “Why”—is responsible for emotions and decision-making but doesn’t process language. In contrast, the neocortex—aligned with the “What”—handles rational thinking and language.

The brain region that governs decisions lacks the ability to process language. People tend to make choices based on emotion and later rationalise them with logic. Starting with “Why” taps into the limbic brain, fostering stronger emotional engagement.

Craft messages that resonate emotionally with your audience. Use the Golden Circle’s biological alignment to spark motivation and connection.

Make your purpose (WHY) clear and communicate it often. Put in place consistent processes that reflect your values. Ensure your actions (WHAT) always align with your purpose and approach.

Additional Activity - Reading - Start With Why by Simon Sinek (Chapter Six)

In this chapter, Sinek argues that trust is built when individuals and organisations are motivated by a purpose beyond self-interest. This alignment of “Why”, “How”, and “What” fosters authenticity and credibility.

Companies focusing solely on “What” they do often struggle to differentiate themselves, becoming trapped in a cycle of feature-matching and selling just a commodity. In contrast, those that lead with “Why” enjoy greater market flexibility and consumer loyalty. For example, Apple’s clear purpose allows it to expand into various product categories, while Dell, defined by its “What”, faces limitations in consumer perception.

Simon also highlights "First Mover Advantage", noting that Creative’s technically superior mp3 player failed to resonate because it was marketed as a product spec (What), whereas Apple’s iPod succeeded by conveying a meaningful benefit (Why).

In hiring, Simon emphasises the importance of recruiting individuals who are passionate about the company’s purpose. Skills and experience should be secondary to cultural fit and belief in the mission. Inspired employees are more productive, innovative, and attract like-minded talent. Additional Activity - Reading - Start With Why by Simon Sinek (Chapter 7)

In this chapter, Sinek discussed Rogers’ Law of Diffusion of Innovations, which explains how new ideas and products spread through society. The bell curve diagram shows how different groups adopt innovations over time: Innovators (2.5%), Early Adopters (13.5%), Early Majority (34%), Late Majority (34%), Laggards (16%)

Example used in the chapter is Apple, where those who camp outside their stores for the latest iPhone are classic early adopters and sit on the left side of the curve. On the far right are the laggards - people who are slow to adopt, often sceptical, and rarely loyal. Businesses should be cautious about investing too much effort in converting this group, as they’re likely to switch brands for a better deal.

The key to long-term success lies in being clear about your purpose - your “Why” - and attracting people who share your beliefs. Once you’ve won over the early adopters and innovators, they’ll help influence the rest to follow.

This can be applied to my role at ARDEX to identify the different types of installers associated with the Diffusion of Innovation groups e.g. working closely with a credible industry installer when promoting a new product towards the early majority.

In this Chapter Sinek explores how organisations lose sight of their original purpose, or WHY. He uses Volkswagen and Walmart as examples. Chapter 8 focuses on the metrics and strategies that increase Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), emphasising long‑term profitability from existing customers over constant acquisition. It outlines some core ways to grow value. Raising prices by communicating added benefits, upselling complementary products, moving customers to higher‑tier offerings through ascension, and boosting purchase frequency with reminders or incentives.

To optimise these efforts, the chapter highlights essential metrics. New lead volume, conversion rates, average transaction value, and the break‑even point. Subscription businesses should also track monthly recurring revenue, churn rate, and overall CLV to understand sustained performance.

A key theme is focusing on your “Tribe”, loyal, high‑value customers who advocate for your brand. These customers yield the greatest returns, while low‑value or resource‑heavy customers may be worth letting go. Finally, the chapter reinforces the importance of Net Promoter Score (NPS), a straightforward measure of customer satisfaction based on likelihood to recommend. Scores above +50 indicate strong advocacy and a healthy customer base.

Moving the forward, the business should focus on gathering NPS from our customers, this could be to find out if they would recommend ARDEX to another trade professional based on products, our technical support services or about our GivBax Rewards loyalty programme. Workplace Learning Reflection – Improving Lead Follow-Up and Tracking Free Resource Downloads

I recently had a discussion with Andy about how we currently manage leads generated through the free resources on the Able Training website. When someone downloads a resource, Sam may follow up with a phone call, and if the call is missed a voicemail is sometimes left asking the individual to call back to explain why they downloaded the resource. During this conversation I reflected on the customer journey and suggested that a more supportive and conversational approach could be more effective. For example, starting a follow-up call by checking whether the person received the resource successfully and asking whether it is useful for the work they are doing. This approach would focus more on helping the individual and understanding their needs, rather than appearing overly sales-driven. Reflecting on this process helped me think more critically about how marketing leads should be nurtured and how communication style can influence engagement with potential customers. (KSB: K1.1, K4.3, S1.1, B2.1)

I also suggested that it would be valuable for us to track the performance of our free resources more closely. For example, measuring how many times each resource is downloaded, how many follow-up calls are made, and how many of these leads eventually convert into enquiries or training bookings. Andy mentioned that it may be possible to gather some of this information using Gemini within our email system. Analysing this data would allow us to better understand which resources are generating the most interest and which topics are most relevant to our audience in the care and education sectors. This would support more data-driven marketing decisions and help us refine our content strategy. (KSB: K1.1, K3.2, S1.3, B4.1)

While we wait for the new CRM system to be implemented, I suggested creating a simple spreadsheet to track free resource leads in the short term. This could include details such as the resource downloaded, the contact information, whether the person has already been contacted, and how many times they have downloaded resources. This would help us avoid repeatedly contacting the same person every time they download something, which could potentially create a negative customer experience. Having this information organised would allow us to manage leads more strategically and improve how we nurture potential enquiries. This discussion demonstrated how marketing processes can be improved through better organisation and data tracking. (KSB: K4.1, S1.3, B2.1, B4.1)

I will also begin drafting a simple spreadsheet to track these leads until the new CRM system is introduced. Instagram Video Performance Analysis and Social Media Content Strategy Review

As part of my marketing role at Able Training, I help create, edit, schedule and promote educational social media content across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and YouTube. Our videos are an important part of our marketing because they allow us to share practical education around areas such as dementia care, behaviour support, health and social care, education and supporting children and young people. Providing useful educational content is an important part of Able Training’s mission and values, while also helping us increase brand awareness, demonstrate our expertise and reach people who may benefit from our knowledge and services.

KSBs: K2.1, S1.3

I identified that despite consistently producing and publishing educational videos over approximately six months, our Instagram Reels were generally receiving much lower reach and engagement than expected, with many achieving approximately 30–200 views. This was particularly noticeable when comparing Instagram with platforms such as TikTok and Facebook, where some of the same educational content has performed better. As part of my responsibility for supporting Able Training’s social media growth, I wanted to understand why Instagram was underperforming rather than continuing to publish content without evaluating its effectiveness. Our aim is not only to provide useful information to our existing followers, but also to reach new audiences and grow Able Training’s presence on Instagram.

KSBs: K2.1, S5.1, B1.1

I carried out a detailed review of our Instagram performance. I first checked the account status and recommendation eligibility to establish whether there were any restrictions that could be limiting our reach. I then reviewed the insights from a selection of individual Reels and compared metrics including views, accounts reached, average watch time, skip rate, likes, comments, shares, saves, follows and sources of views such as the Reels tab, Explore and Feed. I deliberately compared lower-performing videos with a higher-performing Reel so that I could identify differences in how Instagram was distributing the content and how audiences were responding to it.

KSBs: S5.1

My analysis showed that the account did not have any restrictions limiting its reach and that Instagram was recommending some of our content beyond our existing followers. However, I identified significant differences in audience behaviour between videos. For example, one Reel with 144 views achieved an average watch time of 17 seconds and a 38.9% skip rate, whereas another with only 41 views achieved an average watch time of four seconds and a 51.4% skip rate. I also analysed one of our strongest Reels, which had achieved more than 1,500 views. Although Instagram distributed this video much more widely through the Reels and Explore sections, it had a high skip rate, low average watch time and generated very little engagement or follower growth. This helped me understand that views alone should not be used to determine whether social media content has successfully contributed towards our wider marketing objectives.

KSBs: S5.1, K2.1

Through comparing the results, I identified several factors that may be contributing to our Instagram performance. These included the length of our videos, how quickly we capture attention, the clarity and specificity of the opening hook, how quickly the educational value is delivered and whether viewers are given a strong enough reason to save, share or follow after watching. I also considered that Able Training creates content for several different audiences, including parents, carers, educators and health and social care professionals. This highlighted the importance of making the intended audience and subject of each video immediately clear, particularly when Instagram recommends our content to people who may not already know Able Training.

KSBs: S5.1, S1.1, K2.1

Based on my findings, I developed a plan to test a more platform-specific approach to Instagram rather than assuming that the same video format will perform equally well across every social media channel. For our next set of content, I plan to test shorter Instagram edits where appropriate, stronger and more specific opening hooks, quicker delivery of the key educational message and clearer practical takeaways that viewers may want to save or share. Longer versions can continue to be used on platforms where they are more appropriate. This will allow us to maintain the educational value of our content while adapting how it is presented to suit different audience behaviours across each platform.

KSBs: S1.1, S1.3, B1.1

I will monitor the performance of the next set of Instagram Reels and compare the results against our previous content. Rather than focusing only on total views, I will monitor average watch time, skip rate, non-follower reach, saves, shares, engagement and followers generated. This will help me establish whether the changes improve our ability to reach and engage a wider Instagram audience. I can then use the results to make further evidence-based improvements to Able Training’s social media strategy rather than making decisions based on assumptions.

Able Weekly Newsletter Development, Performance Review & Content Strategy


Today I reviewed the performance of recent Able Training email newsletters before developing this week’s Able Weekly campaign.

I analysed recent Mailchimp campaign data, including total open rates, human open rates and click rates. I compared several previous campaigns to identify patterns in performance and looked more closely at one of our strongest-performing newsletters, which achieved a 33% human open rate. I reviewed its subject line, preview text, structure, length and content to identify what may have contributed to its stronger engagement.

This helped me recognise that our audience appears to respond well to subject lines that either create curiosity or communicate a clear benefit, rather than simply listing what is included in the newsletter. I also reviewed the impact of Apple Mail Privacy Protection and automated bot activity on our reported statistics so that future performance comparisons can be based on more reliable human engagement data.

Using these findings, I changed the approach to this week’s newsletter. Rather than following the same predictable structure of leading with a resource or podcast, I created a more personal opening around a quote that had generated discussion within the Able office. I then included updates about Andy representing Able Training at professional events, upcoming speaking engagements, the latest podcast episode, the Resource Library and relevant training opportunities.

I deliberately included more behind-the-scenes content about the people and work behind Able Training. The aim was to make the newsletter feel less like a collection of promotional updates and more like communication from a real team, helping subscribers understand our work, values and expertise while still providing useful information and clear calls to action.

I also refined the newsletter to keep sections concise and easy to scan, while ensuring there was content relevant to our different audiences across Health, Social Care, Education, carers and families.

After reviewing the finished newsletter, Andy gave positive feedback and said it looked “fantastic”, was “really good” and congratulated me on the work.

What I learned

This activity helped me understand the importance of using campaign data to inform content decisions rather than relying solely on assumptions about what subscribers will engage with.

I learned that headline open-rate figures can be misleading because automated opens and clicks can inflate results. Reviewing human engagement data gave me a more realistic benchmark for our campaigns and will help me make more accurate comparisons in future.

I also learned that newsletter performance is not only about individual pieces of content. Subject lines, preview text, content hierarchy, length, tone and how personal the communication feels can all influence engagement.

Reviewing one of our strongest previous campaigns showed me that audiences may respond well to useful, benefit-led messaging as well as curiosity-driven subject lines. This has encouraged me to vary our approach rather than using the same style each week.

How this will improve my future work

Going forward, I will monitor human open rates, click rates and individual link performance rather than relying only on overall open rates.

I will continue testing different subject-line approaches, including curiosity-led, benefit-led and reflective/question-based messaging, and compare the results over time.

I will also continue developing Able Weekly so that it balances useful educational content, commercial opportunities and more personal behind-the-scenes updates. This should help strengthen the relationship between Able Training and its subscribers, increase engagement with our free resources and podcast content, and ultimately support enquiries and lead generation for our training services.

During a meeting at work with my marketing manager, we discussed my recent learnings on the course about managing our product portfolio and identifying which of the wider products we offer as a B2B business fit into the BCG Matrix. 

We first looked at the two criteria for the matrix: Market share, or how much of the market your product captures, and Market growth rate, which looks at how fast the market is growing. 

Dogs. These products are in a weak position of low growth and low market share. They typically generate low or negative profit and use up more resources than they return. 

In my event portfolio, I used an example of an event that we had discontinued, WORKTECH Auckland. This annual event had been losing money for 2-3 years, and despite efforts to revive it with different marketing strategies, constant research and product development, and manipulating price and promotion, the event was deemed a failure and was removed from the portfolio of events. 

In the other team (EMEA), they highlighted WORKTECH Berlin as a dog. This event is still running, despite the breaking-even or losses incurred since 2022. The event's failures have been due to various factors: a small city, a poor database of contacts, poor partnerships in the region, low investment in marketing, delays in event confirmation, which has previously led to a short marketing campaign cycle, and lack of understanding of the region's needs in terms of learning and experience at a future of work event. 

In conclusion, we thought that a lot of time and research should be spent deciding which events to run each year, and not just going with the previous year's calendar. Critiquing the choice of events to ensure their future success is a must for all event organisers. 

Cashcow. These products have a low market growth but a high market share. They are typically mature, reliable products that are usually profitable and could be in a stable or slow-growing market. Cashcows need defending, but not aggressive investment, and their profits can be used to fund other ventures. 

In my event portfolio, I used WORKTECH New York as an example. It's a popular event, regularly sells a healthy number of tickets, and hits its sponsorship targets each year. The event creates a lot of traction around the dates when they're confirmed, from other investors and stakeholders, to maximise their opportunities. 

In the other team, they run one of our biggest events in the calendar, and the event that kickstarted the company, WORKTECH London. In previous years, this was a cash cow, a regular, reliable banker of revenue for the company. In more recent years, the event has run at losses and the event team has really struggled to fill out the conference room with the relevant contacts. 

To conclude our review of these products, a closer eye on the profitability should be kept up with, and regular reviews and improvements should be made to ensure the event's success. Marketing strategies may need to be adjusted and more innovative ideas implemented to ensure this event's future success. 

Question marks. High market growth but a low market share. These are products in a booming market, but the product's share is small, perhaps due to other brands in the space or it being a newer entry to the market. Their success is uncertain. 

An example in my event portfolio is a new event we launched last year, but postponed to 2026 due to time constraints and low sign-ups from attendees and sponsors, which is typical for a question mark event. The event is far from the usual products we sell and was based around a government announcement of Manchester being named the new AI city in the North, which never came. The target customer is still unclear, the sponsorship engagement is poor, and changes to the format and programme of content may be made to move closer to the typical WORKTECH event framework. This event is a big gamble, one that requires support, investment, of time and money, and buy-in from the team to ensure its success. These conversations are currently live in my day-to-day activities, but using this reflection will certainly help with the discussions and decisions being made. 

The other event team has also looked at a new event location in Poland, where the event conference series has not taken place before. The event idea is in the early stages, but with the discussions we've had, an emphasis on planning, preparation, research, and a thorough marketing strategy should be discussed with the stakeholders before the new event is confirmed. 

In conclusion, these are exciting new products aiming to penetrate existing or new markets, and aslong as sufficient research takes place, they could become very profitable and a successful part of the business portfolio. 

Stars. High market growth and a high market share. These products are leaders in a growing market; they often require a heavy investment, but also generate a lot of revenue. 

A star product in my portfolio is our Financial Workplace New York event. It's a vertical targeting the financial sector and hosted in New York. Running off the back of the cash cow event, WORKTECH New York, where we knew we had a strong database of contacts, strong brand recognition, and a solid network, moving into a niche vertical was a strong move. The event pulls a great deal of interest from sponsors looking to work with financial firms, which came off the back of post-COVID, where legal and finance kept running and turning profits. This event has been replicated in London and will be trialled in other financial cities in the hope of creating more star events.

WORKTECH Events (1-day future of work and workplace)
Customer segments: Senior workplace leaders from HR, CRE, IT, FM, and A+D
USP: Global learning and a strong network of expert speakers
Pricing model: Tiered pricing from Super Early Bird to Early Bird and Standard rate, with some other discounts available
Indicative price: Base price shown is $549, with a standard price of $649

Here are the top 6 competitors in the US, their customer segments, USP, pricing model, prices, and how they compare to WORKTECH events:

1) CoreNet Global – North America Summit (CRE end-users + service partners)
Customer segments: Corporate Real Estate (end-users), workplace leaders, plus major CRE suppliers/service providers.
USP: Flagship CRE association summit; big networking + membership-driven community.
Pricing model: High-price, tiered registration with member vs non-member price visibility.
Indicative price: Base price shown: $2,835 for a 3-day pass.May include other networking/workshop events.
Compared to WORKTECH: Competes for senior CRE time/budget but is a very different spend level (often paid via professional development budgets).

2) IFMA – World Workplace (FM / workplace operations + expo)
Customer segments: Facilities Management leaders, workplace operations, service providers; strong expo draw.
USP: “Premier FM conference + expo” with a large vendor ecosystem and education.
Pricing model: Multi-tiered (presale → tiers) + member vs regular + daily vs full event.
Indicative prices (2026 reg form): Full Event: $800–$1,225 (member), $1,000–$1,425 (regular); Daily $450–$875 (member), $550–$975 (regular). A 3-day event that includes networking events throughout.
Compared to WORKTECH: Still pricier than you, but closer—WORKTECH can position as more boutique/curated (and easier to get approved).

3) SHRM – Annual Conference (HR mega-conference)
Customer segments: HR leaders, People/DEI, talent, generalist HR; huge scale.
USP: Largest HR conference positioning; broad HR education + expo.
Pricing model: Tiered (Preview/Early/Standard/On-site) + member/nonmember.
Indicative prices (SHRM26): $2,095 preview, $2,395 early bird, $2,595 standard, $2,695 on-site (member pricing shown; nonmember higher). A 4-day conference with networking events. 
Compared to WORKTECH: Different category (mega). Your pricing is far more accessible, but SHRM competes for calendar space for HR/People leaders.

4) HR Technology Conference (HRIT buyers + vendors)
Customer segments: HR tech buyers, HR leaders evaluating tools, HRIT teams; heavy vendor/expo.
USP: Large HR tech marketplace + sessions; very vendor-driven.
Pricing model: Conference pass with discount pricing; team bundles.
Indicative prices (Oct 2026): $1,295 (discount) / $1,995 (list) for a conference pass. The ticket includes networking events and social activities. 
Compared to WORKTECH: More “buying software” oriented and expensive; you can win by emphasizing strategic workplace transformation + cross-discipline (CRE/Workplace/Tech/HR).

5) Future of Work USA (Dallas) – HR/EX/Digital Workplace focus
Customer segments: HR/People, EX, Internal Comms, Digital Workplace.
USP: Track-based agenda; strong HR/EX orientation.
Pricing model: Pass tiers (Bronze/Silver/Gold) with early bird pricing.

Customer segments: CRE owners/investors/developers + brokers; some corporate CRE depending on topic.
USP: Local market specificity + frequent events.
Pricing model: Lower-cost tickets, often with tiered pricing as inventory moves.

Compared to WORKTECH: Not the same “future of work” format, but competes for CRE attention with cheap, local, frequent options.

Building Brand Awareness Through Media and Association Partnerships
Project Overview

As part of my role supporting the promotion of WORKTECH events in Australia, I led an initiative to increase brand awareness and credibility by developing relationships with relevant media outlets and professional associations across New South Wales and Victoria.

The objective of this project was to expand the event’s visibility within key professional communities and strengthen brand trust in the Australian market. This involved identifying relevant industry organisations and publications, researching potential partners, and establishing media and community partnerships to support event promotion.

Historically, WORKTECH events in Australia had secured between two and four media or association partners. My aim was to maintain this benchmark while also improving the relevance and strategic value of these partnerships by targeting organisations that closely aligned with the event’s audience and industry positioning.

Strategic Thinking and Link to the 7Ps

This campaign aligned with several elements of the 7Ps marketing framework, particularly Promotion, Place, People and Physical Evidence.

Promotion

Media partnerships were used as a promotional strategy to expand the event’s reach through trusted industry platforms. By collaborating with respected publications and associations, the campaign leveraged existing audiences rather than relying solely on paid advertising or internal databases.

This approach helped position the event within established professional networks, increasing visibility among relevant decision-makers.

Place

The partnerships also supported the “Place” element of the marketing mix by distributing event information through channels already used by the target audience. Industry associations, professional groups and trade media act as important discovery platforms for B2B professionals seeking events, insights and networking opportunities.

This ensured that event promotion appeared within the spaces where potential delegates already consume industry information.

People

Relationship building was a critical component of this project. Establishing connections with editors, association managers and industry representatives required strong communication and stakeholder engagement skills.

These relationships contribute to long-term brand equity and may support future collaborations, including speaker opportunities, cross-promotional activity or industry partnerships.

Physical Evidence

Association partnerships also act as credibility signals. When respected organisations support or promote an event, it reinforces the legitimacy and authority of the brand. This is particularly important when building awareness in markets where the brand may still be developing recognition.

Featuring association logos and media partners on promotional materials strengthens perceived trust and professionalism.

Execution of the Campaign

To implement this project, I carried out the following steps:

• Researched relevant professional associations and industry publications across NSW and Victoria
• Identified organisations aligned with workplace strategy, corporate real estate, HR, technology and design sectors
• Developed a shortlist of potential partners based on audience relevance and credibility
• Initiated outreach to editors, association managers and community leaders
• Presented collaboration opportunities including event promotion, content sharing and community engagement
• Coordinated agreements with selected partners and ensured their promotion was integrated into the campaign timeline

Through this process, I personally managed the outreach, relationship development and coordination of promotional partnerships.

Rationale for This Approach

This approach was chosen because media and association partnerships can significantly amplify brand reach in a cost-effective way. Rather than relying entirely on paid media, these collaborations provide access to established professional audiences who already trust the partner organisation.

For B2B events such as WORKTECH, credibility and industry authority are key drivers of delegate decision-making. Being associated with respected industry bodies helps reinforce the event’s reputation and positioning as a thought leadership platform.

This strategy also supports long-term brand development by embedding the event within relevant professional communities.

Potential Risks and Mitigation

One potential risk is partnering with organisations that do not closely align with the event’s target audience. This could result in limited engagement or ineffective promotion.

To mitigate this risk, I prioritised partners with strong relevance to workplace strategy, corporate real estate, HR and technology sectors.

Another risk is that partnerships may not deliver the expected promotional support. To address this, clear expectations and promotional deliverables were discussed during the collaboration process.

Finally, there is a risk that too many partnerships could dilute the perceived exclusivity of the event. For this reason, I focused on securing a smaller number of high-quality partners rather than pursuing large volumes of collaborations.

Expected Outcomes

The expected outcomes of this initiative include:

• Increased brand visibility within key professional communities
• Greater credibility through association with respected industry organisations
• Increased website traffic and event enquiries from partner channels
• Improved delegate acquisition through trusted referral sources
• Long-term relationship development with industry networks

This strategy supports both short-term event promotion and long-term brand positioning within the Australian workplace and real estate sectors.

Reflection on Learning

This project strengthened my understanding of how relationship-based marketing and community engagement can complement traditional promotional channels. It also reinforced the importance of strategic partner selection to ensure alignment with brand positioning and target audiences.

Through leading the research, outreach and coordination of these partnerships, I developed practical experience in stakeholder management, B2B relationship building and integrated campaign planning.

Campaign Structure: Six Key Phases

• Pre-Launch
• Super Early Bird
• Early Bird
• Standard Rate
• Conversion Drive
• Post-Event

Each phase included a defined time frame, objectives and key actions required to support successful campaign delivery.

This structure allows the team to clearly understand the purpose of each stage in the campaign lifecycle and ensures that marketing activities are strategically sequenced rather than delivered reactively.

Product:
Each phase emphasises the value of the event through speaker announcements, agenda releases and thought-leadership content that demonstrate the event’s relevance and insight.

Price:
Ticket pricing phases such as super early bird and early bird are used strategically to incentivise early commitment and maintain sales momentum.

Place:

Promotion:
Marketing communications evolve throughout the campaign phases, moving from awareness and thought leadership in early stages to urgency and conversion messaging closer to the event date.

People:
The roadmap highlights collaboration between marketing, sales, and partnerships teams. For example, VIP outreach and sponsor engagement activities are coordinated with the sales team to maximise delegate acquisition.

Process:
By mapping activities week by week, the roadmap improves campaign coordination, helping the team manage deadlines, content delivery and communication sequencing.

Physical Evidence:

• VIP outreach programmes
• Collaboration with sponsors and partners
• Direct marketing and personalised communications

I also incorporated activities involving multidisciplinary teams, including collaboration with the sales team to support sponsor engagement and outreach to high-value prospects.

By consolidating these activities into one central roadmap, the team now has a clearer view of how different functions contribute to overall campaign performance.

Supporting Campaign Performance

Recognising that not all events consistently reach their delegate targets, I also included additional strategies to support campaigns during critical stages. These recommendations were designed to help the team respond proactively when ticket sales slow.

Examples include:

• Increased personalised outreach to high-value prospects
• Targeted group ticket offers
• Increased direct marketing activity
• Additional collaboration with sponsors and partners to extend reach
• Enhanced segmentation and messaging

These ideas were included to provide the team with practical options for improving conversion and maintaining campaign momentum.

Outcomes and Benefits for the Team

The roadmap provides the team with a clear, structured campaign framework that improves visibility, coordination and strategic alignment across event marketing activities.

By linking campaign actions directly to sales targets and delegate progression, the plan helps the team better monitor performance and identify when adjustments may be required.

It also supports knowledge sharing by documenting best practices and successful campaign approaches that can be applied across multiple events.

Leading this project strengthened my understanding of campaign planning, strategic marketing coordination and the importance of aligning marketing activity with commercial outcomes.

By developing this roadmap and sharing it with colleagues, I was able to contribute to a more consistent and collaborative approach to event marketing within the team. My aim was to create a resource that not only supports current campaigns but also helps colleagues plan future events more effectively.

Throughout the project, I ensured my work remained inclusive and professional by engaging with team members across different functions, incorporating their insights and recognising the collaborative nature of successful event delivery.

This experience reinforced the value of structured marketing processes, cross-team communication and data-driven planning in delivering successful campaigns.

Project Summary: Buyer Funnel to Loyalty Loop Presentation

This project focused on developing and delivering a strategic presentation to the WORKTECH events team, designed to shift internal thinking from a traditional buyer funnel approach to a customer decision journey and loyalty loop model.

The objective was to help the team better understand how delegates and sponsors make decisions, and to highlight the commercial importance of post-purchase stages such as experience, loyalty, and advocacy. The presentation introduced the concept that customers do not move linearly from awareness to purchase, but instead move in and out of consideration, influenced by trust, peer recommendation, and perceived value.

To support this, I analysed internal data across three key markets (London, New York, and Sydney), assessing both delegate and sponsor behaviour. The analysis showed that while WORKTECH is strong at attracting new audiences, repeat attendance and long-term loyalty are relatively low for delegates, and moderate but inconsistent for sponsors. This demonstrated a clear opportunity to build stronger ongoing relationships.

The presentation also incorporated external research, including McKinsey insights on word-of-mouth influence and referral marketing performance, to reinforce the importance of advocacy in driving growth.

Finally, I will facilitate a team discussion using structured, open-ended questions to encourage cross-functional input from marketing, sales, production, and operations. The focus is on identifying how WORKTECH could enhance customer experience, increase repeat engagement, and create advocates who contribute to long-term event growth.

Reflection & Evaluation

This project was effective in combining both strategic theory and practical business insight. By using internal data alongside established marketing models, I was able to present a balanced and credible argument that resonated with the wider team.

One of the key strengths of this work was the ability to translate complex marketing concepts into a format that was accessible and relevant to a non-marketing audience. The use of real WORKTECH data made the insights tangible and helped position the discussion as a commercial opportunity rather than a critique of current activity.

The comparison across markets was particularly valuable, as it demonstrated that while loyalty varies, it is achievable, and therefore something the business can actively influence. Additionally, identifying differences between delegate and sponsor behaviour highlighted an opportunity to apply successful relationship-building strategies more consistently across both audiences.

Facilitating the discussion will develop my confidence in leading strategic conversations. I will ensure the tone remains positive and collaborative, encouraging contributions from different departments while guiding the conversation back to customer experience and long-term value rather than tactical execution.

Areas for Improvement

While the presentation is strong, one area for improvement would be to incorporate more real-time customer insight, such as direct feedback or testimonials, to further strengthen the emotional connection to the customer journey.

In the future, I would also look to:

Track and measure changes in retention and engagement following this discussion
Develop specific test initiatives to improve loyalty and advocacy
Align more closely with sales and operations to ensure a consistent post-event experience

Key Learning: This project reinforced that:

Marketing is not just about acquisition, but about building long-term value through relationships
Customer experience plays a critical role in influencing repeat behaviour and advocacy
Data-driven insights are essential for influencing internal stakeholders and driving strategic change

WORKTECH Events & WORKTECH Academy Integration Workshop

As part of a Marketing and Sales Leadership Team workshop, I participated in discussions focused on the future relationship between WORKTECH Events and WORKTECH Academy. The objective of the workshop was to explore how the two businesses could work more effectively together to improve customer value, engagement, and commercial performance.

The workshop included analysis of customer research, survey findings, stakeholder feedback, and business priorities. Discussions initially focused on packaging and commercial offers; however, the research highlighted that the more important challenge was understanding how the two businesses should connect and complement one another rather than simply creating bundled products.

A key learning from the workshop was the distinction between connecting customer experiences and bundling products. The evidence suggested that customers value flexibility and clear purpose, with many preferring to purchase events and Academy products separately while remaining open to a more connected experience.

Three strategic opportunities were identified:

1. Creating a Clear Customer Journey from Events to Academy

The workshop highlighted the need for a structured pathway that guides event attendees towards Academy engagement through a series of touchpoints, including:

Post-event summaries
Research reports
Briefings and roundtables
Academy membership

This would create a more intentional customer journey and increase engagement between annual events.

2. Supporting Year-Round Engagement

Customer feedback demonstrated demand for structured interactions between events, including:

Briefings
Quarterly reports
Roundtables
Curated peer discussions

Importantly, research indicated that customers preferred organised, high-value touchpoints rather than always-on online communities.

3. Protecting the Academy's Trusted Voice

One of the strongest findings from the research was the value customers place on WORKTECH Academy's independence and credibility. Participants consistently highlighted the importance of:

Honest discussion
Practical lessons learned
Sharing failures as well as successes

The workshop identified that maintaining editorial independence would be critical if Academy and Events become more closely connected.

Additional discussion focused on:

Audience segmentation
Different sponsor needs and motivations
Membership value propositions
Shared ownership and accountability
The need for common customer data and measurement frameworks

The recommended direction was to connect the two offers through customer experience and engagement rather than merge them into a single commercial package.

Reflection

This workshop provided valuable insight into the relationship between customer research, brand positioning, and business strategy.

One of my key learnings was that organisational priorities do not always align with customer priorities. The initial focus of the workshop centred on pricing, packaging, and commercial opportunities because these are areas that businesses can directly control. However, the research suggested that customers were more interested in clarity, trust, and meaningful engagement than in bundled commercial offers.

The strongest finding from the research was the importance of trust and authenticity. Customers consistently valued WORKTECH's ability to provide independent, candid insight rather than heavily commercialised content. This reinforced the importance of protecting brand credibility when developing future products, partnerships, and marketing activity.

I also gained a greater appreciation for customer journey design. The discussion highlighted that customer engagement should not be viewed as a series of disconnected transactions, but as an ongoing relationship that develops over time through relevant touchpoints and valuable experiences.

The workshop is strongly linked to previous work I completed on the Customer Decision Journey and Loyalty Loop. Many of the recommendations reflected the same principles of retention, engagement, advocacy, and long-term customer value.

Going forward, I would like to develop my understanding of:

Membership and community business models
Customer lifecycle management
Customer experience strategy
Cross-functional planning and governance
Measuring long-term customer engagement

Overall, this activity strengthened my understanding of how customer insight can inform strategic decision-making and demonstrated the importance of balancing commercial objectives with customer trust and brand integrity.

Using CRM Data for Financial Workplace Frankfurt

As part of the marketing preparation for Financial Workplace Frankfurt, I used our CRM to identify relevant financial-sector contacts for a targeted pre-launch campaign.

The objective was to find previous attendees and past speakers from other Financial Workplace events, particularly London and New York, and use this existing relationship data to support the Frankfurt launch.

A Call for Speakers email to relevant past speakers and senior contacts
A Save the Date email to previous attendees and other suitable financial workplace contacts
Process
1. Define the target audience

I first clarified the type of contacts we wanted to reach, focusing on people with previous engagement in Financial Workplace events.

This included:

Past attendees
Past speakers
Senior workplace and corporate real estate professionals
Contacts working within financial services organisations
Relevant contacts from previous London and New York Financial Workplace events

Previous event attendance
Speaker history
Organisation
Job title and seniority
Industry
Geographic relevance
Previous relationship with WORKTECH

This helped me build a more accurate picture of the audience and identify contacts who already had familiarity with the Financial Workplace proposition.

3. Segment the audience

I separated the contacts into appropriate campaign groups rather than using one message for everyone.

For example:

Past speakers and relevant senior contacts could receive the Call for Speakers communication because they already had experience contributing to WORKTECH content.

Past attendees could receive the Save the Date communication, with messaging focused on the launch of Frankfurt and their existing connection with Financial Workplace.

This segmentation allowed the messaging and call-to-action to be more relevant to each group.

Whether contact details were current
Whether the individual was still in a relevant role

5. Develop the campaign journey

I then considered how the contacts should move through the early event marketing journey.

The first communication would focus on speaker participation, giving relevant contacts the opportunity to contribute to the programme.

This would then be followed by a broader Save the Date communication to maintain awareness and introduce the Frankfurt event ahead of the main campaign launch.

Using this staged approach allows WORKTECH to begin building interest before the full programme is available.

6. Use CRM insight to support personalisation

The CRM information could also be used to make communications more relevant.

For example, previous speakers can be approached differently from someone who has only attended an event, while previous Financial Workplace attendees can be contacted with greater context because they already understand the format and subject area.

This demonstrates how CRM data can support personalisation without needing to create completely individual campaigns for every contact.

7. Measure and refine

Once the campaign is sent, I would review performance including:

Email opens
Click-through rates
Speaker responses
Save the Date engagement
Registrations or enquiries generated
Performance between different audience segments

These insights could then be used to refine future communications and identify which groups are most engaged with Financial Workplace Frankfurt.

This activity demonstrated how CRM technology can support much more than storing customer information. By using historical attendance, speaker relationships, company information and engagement data, I was able to create a more targeted campaign for a new event.

The task also reinforced the importance of segmentation. Separating past speakers from previous attendees allowed the communication to reflect the customer's previous relationship with WORKTECH and provide a more appropriate next step in their journey.

This was a practical example of using CRM data to support targeting, personalisation, customer journey planning and campaign measurement, rather than relying on broad database marketing.

Webinar Learning Summary: Your Customer Journey Isn’t Linear Anymore
Summary of Learning

I attended the webinar “Your Customer Journey Isn’t Linear Anymore - Is Your Marketing Keeping Up?”, which focused on how modern customer journeys are becoming increasingly fragmented across websites, digital channels and marketing touchpoints.

A key learning was that marketers cannot control the exact route a customer takes, but they can influence how connected and consistent the overall experience feels.

The session reinforced that customers may move backwards and forwards between different touchpoints, rather than following a simple linear funnel. Because of this, marketing activity should make it easy for customers to:

Discover the organisation
Understand its value
Build trust
Identify a relevant next step
Move between channels without experiencing a disconnected journey

A central message from the webinar was that the customer journey may be fragmented, but the customer experience should not feel fragmented.

Application to My Role

This learning is particularly relevant to WORKTECH because our customers may interact with the brand through multiple channels before taking action.

For example, a potential delegate may first see a LinkedIn post, later receive an email, visit an event page, read a piece of thought leadership, engage with a speaker or sponsor, and only then decide to book.

This means each touchpoint should support the same overall brand experience and make the next step clear.

The session also reinforced the importance of ensuring that website content, email marketing, social media and event messaging are aligned rather than operating separately.

Reflection

The webinar strengthened my understanding that customer journey planning should focus less on forcing customers through a fixed funnel and more on creating a connected experience across different channels.

It also linked closely to previous learning I have completed around CRM, segmentation, analytics and customer journeys. Data can help identify how customers interact with different touchpoints, while marketing teams can use those insights to reduce friction and improve the experience.

A key takeaway for me is that consistency, trust and clarity are important throughout the journey. Even if customers take different routes, each interaction should reinforce the same value proposition and help them move towards an appropriate next action.

Going forward, I would like to review WORKTECH campaigns from a customer journey perspective and identify where customers may experience gaps between email, social media, website content and event registration.
