Summary of Activity

As part of improving sponsor marketing across WORKTECH events, I created a structured Event Partnership Timeline to give sponsors and internal teams a clearer view of when promotional activity should take place before, during, and after an event.

The purpose of the timeline was to improve coordination between marketing, sales, account managers, and sponsors by setting clearer expectations around:

When sponsor collateral should be supplied
When sponsor announcements should begin
When sponsors should promote the event through their own channels
When speaker and session promotion should take place
When direct attendee outreach should happen
How sponsor activity should increase as the event approaches
What post-event activity should continue after the conference

The timeline was structured around key milestones from approximately 12 weeks before the event through to two weeks after, helping activity build progressively rather than happening all at once.

Planning the Sponsor Journey

The timeline considered how sponsor promotion should develop alongside the wider event marketing campaign.

At around 12 weeks out, activity focuses on visibility and awareness, including sponsorship announcements, social media activity, and identifying opportunities to use sponsor networks.

As the event approaches, activity becomes more focused on engagement and conversion. This includes promoting speaker participation, including sponsors in email campaigns, encouraging sponsor outreach to target attendees, and sharing milestone content such as agenda previews and brochures.

Closer to the event, sponsors are encouraged to increase visibility through social media, event attendance graphics, exhibitor promotion, and direct engagement with delegates.

The event day activity then focuses on maximising the partnership through networking, branding, speaking opportunities, demonstrations, and delegate interaction.

Finally, the timeline includes post-event activity such as follow-up communications, event reports, sponsor recognition, feedback meetings, and opportunities to continue the relationship beyond the event.

Stakeholder Collaboration

Developing the timeline required discussion with the sales team because sponsor expectations are often set during the sales and contracting process.

We discussed what marketing needed from sponsors and when those materials would be required so that the sales team could communicate these expectations more clearly during sponsor conversations.

This also allowed the team to consider how sponsor agreements and account management discussions could better reflect the promotional responsibilities of both WORKTECH and the sponsor.

Creating this shared structure helped improve alignment between departments and reduced the risk of sponsors providing materials too late for them to be used effectively.

Business Value

The timeline provides several benefits to WORKTECH:

Creates clearer expectations for sponsors
Improves coordination between marketing and sales
Helps sponsors maximise the value of their partnership
Reduces last-minute requests for collateral
Creates more consistent sponsor visibility throughout the campaign
Aligns sponsor activity with wider event marketing milestones
Encourages sponsors to use their own audiences and networks to extend reach
Supports stronger post-event relationship management

It also helps ensure sponsor activity contributes to the natural build-up of excitement around the event rather than competing with or duplicating other marketing activity.

Reflection

This activity strengthened my understanding of partnership marketing and the importance of coordinating multiple stakeholders within an event campaign.

A key learning was that sponsors should not simply be treated as organisations that appear on an event website. They can also act as marketing partners with their own networks, speakers, audiences, and communication channels.

I also recognised the importance of setting expectations early. If promotional requirements are only discussed close to the event, there is less opportunity to use sponsor content effectively. Creating a structured timeline allows both WORKTECH and sponsors to plan activity more strategically.

The process also reinforced the value of cross-department collaboration. Marketing activity is influenced by conversations that begin much earlier within sales, so ensuring that both teams understand the timeline improves the customer experience and makes partnership delivery more consistent.

Going forward, I would like to review the timeline after several events and gather feedback from sponsors, sales, and marketing to identify which activities generate the strongest engagement and where the process could be improved further.

Q2: Macro Environment Analysis: PESTLE Factors


Knowledge (What you need to know in UK insurance)

Competitor & Microenvironment Analysis

Understand the purpose of competitor analysis in insurance: monitoring competitors’ products, pricing, and claims practices to adjust strategies quickly.

Know the microenvironment factors in insurance: competitors, brokers, customers, reinsurers, and suppliers.

Recognize the macroenvironment factors using PESTLE that can affect insurance: economic cycles, social trends, technology, legal and regulatory changes.

PESTLE Analysis Applied to Insurance

Economic → inflation, interest rates, consumer affordability, and premium pricing.

Social → demographic trends, health and wellness awareness, lifestyle changes affecting life, health, and general insurance products.

Political & Legal → FCA/PRA regulations, solvency requirements, insurance law, and compliance standards.

Technological → digital platforms for policy management, claims automation, InsurTech innovations.

Environmental → climate change, natural disasters, ESG considerations affecting underwriting.

Market Trends & Risks in Insurance

Identify opportunities and threats from emerging risks: cyber insurance, climate risk, health trends.

Understand how competitor offerings influence market share and customer retention.

Skills (What you need to be able to do in insurance)

Analytical Skills

Assess competitor insurance products, pricing, and claims performance.

Interpret PESTLE factors to predict impacts on underwriting, claims, and product development.

Decision-Making & Strategy

Adjust underwriting, claims management, and marketing strategies based on competitor and market insights.

Identify gaps in the market and propose solutions (new products, better service, competitive pricing).

Market Awareness

Monitor trends affecting policyholders: health, lifestyle, economic shifts, and emerging risks.

Track competitor innovations in the UK insurance sector to maintain competitiveness.

Communication & Reporting

Present findings on competitors, risks, and trends to colleagues, management, or brokers.

Advise clients and stakeholders based on current market conditions and regulatory environment.

Behaviour (How you act in the insurance market)

Proactive & Adaptive

Respond quickly to competitor pricing, product launches, and regulatory changes.

Anticipate market trends that could impact premiums, claims, or customer needs.

Analytical & Detail-Oriented

Examine market, competitor, and PESTLE data carefully before recommending actions.

Ensure underwriting and claims decisions reflect accurate risk assessments.

Customer-Focused

Align insurance solutions with customer needs, affordability, and risk profile.

Use social and economic insights to enhance client service and retention.

Professional & Ethical

Comply with FCA, PRA, and GDPR regulations.

Ensure all market intelligence, competitor analysis, and client advice meet ethical standards.

Q3:Tool – Porter’s Five Forces

Knowledge (What you need to know)

Competitive Environment & Micro Environment

Understand the micro environment: customers, competitors, suppliers (insurance carriers, technology providers), and stakeholders (regulators, employees, media).

Know how competitor behavior, customer preferences, and supplier terms influence UK insurance brokerage operations.

Recognize direct competitors (other brokers, insurers) and indirect competitors (InsurTech platforms, online comparison sites).

Porter’s Five Forces in Insurance

Competitive rivalry: High competition among UK brokers and insurers.

Threat of new entrants: Impact of new brokers or digital insurers entering the market.

Threat of substitutes: Direct-to-consumer insurers, comparison websites, or alternative risk solutions.

Bargaining power of suppliers: Influence of insurance carriers and reinsurers on product pricing and availability.

Bargaining power of buyers: Customers’ ability to switch insurers or demand better premiums and coverage.

PESTLE Analysis & Macro Environment

Political/Legal: FCA and PRA regulations, compliance, data protection (GDPR).

Economic: Inflation, interest rates, and consumer affordability affecting insurance premiums.

Social: Customer trends, lifestyle changes, sustainability awareness.

Technological: Digital platforms, InsurTech, claims automation.

Environmental: Climate change, natural disasters, ESG considerations.

Strategic Responses

Understand how UK insurance firms respond to competition: brand loyalty, service differentiation, pricing strategies, and creating barriers to entry.

Skills (What you need to be able to do)

Market & Competitor Analysis

Apply Porter’s Five Forces to assess competitive intensity in the UK insurance market.

Identify competitor strengths, weaknesses, pricing strategies, and market positioning.

Customer & Relationship Management

Evaluate client needs (individuals, SMEs) and tailor insurance products accordingly.

Anticipate buyer demands and maintain strong relationships to reduce churn.

Strategic Decision-Making

Develop strategies to counter new entrants, substitutes, or high buyer power.

Adjust offerings based on competitor analysis and market trends.

Macro Environment Awareness

Use PESTLE insights to forecast regulatory, economic, or social impacts on underwriting, claims, and product development.

Communication & Reporting

Present findings on competitors, threats, and market trends clearly to management or clients.

Behaviour (How you act in the insurance market)

Proactive & Adaptive

Respond quickly to competitor actions, regulatory changes, and market trends.

Anticipate emerging risks or new technologies that could impact the brokerage.

Analytical & Detail-Oriented

Carefully assess competitive forces, customer power, and supplier dynamics before making decisions.

Customer-Focused

Prioritize client needs, affordability, and value-added service.

Build trust and loyalty to reduce the threat of customers switching providers.

Professional & Ethical

Ensure compliance with FCA/PRA regulations and ethical standards.

Maintain transparency and integrity in competitive and customer interactions.

Strategic & Forward-Thinking

Use insights from Porter’s Five Forces and PESTLE to develop sustainable competitive strategies

16.2.2 Public Relations (PR):Study Note – Movo Insurance Brokers and the UK Insurance Industry

Public relations is the management of an organisation’s reputation and its relationships with customers, insurers, employees, regulators and the wider public. Unlike paid advertising, PR seeks to generate trust through positive customer experiences, professional communication, community activity, industry relationships and earned media coverage.

PR is particularly important in the UK insurance industry because customers are purchasing a promise that an insurer will support them if something goes wrong. A broker’s reputation for honesty, expertise and dependable claims support can therefore strongly influence a customer’s choice.

Application to Movo Insurance Brokers

Movo can use PR to strengthen its reputation as a professional, independent and customer-focused insurance broker. Relevant PR activities could include:

Publishing press releases about business growth, new offices, specialist insurance schemes or community partnerships.
Sharing helpful insurance guidance through LinkedIn, the Movo website and trade publications.
Supporting charities, local businesses and networking groups such as BNI.
Publishing positive customer reviews and claims-support success stories, subject to consent and confidentiality.
Commenting on topical risks such as cybercrime, flooding, underinsurance and changes affecting landlords or businesses.
Building professional relationships with insurers, underwriters, trade associations and local media.
Responding promptly and professionally to complaints, negative reviews or significant service issues.

For example, Movo could publish an article explaining how businesses can avoid underinsurance by regularly reviewing their property values, turnover and business interruption indemnity periods. If a local newspaper or trade publication shared the article, this would provide earned exposure while positioning Movo as a knowledgeable and responsible broker.

Crisis communication in insurance

Crisis communication is an important part of PR. Movo may need to communicate following a serious claim, insurer service failure, cyber incident or customer complaint. Communication should be prompt, accurate and empathetic, while avoiding promises about claim outcomes that have not been authorised by the insurer.

Movo must also protect confidential customer information and comply with UK GDPR, FCA requirements and the Consumer Duty. Public communications should be clear, fair and not misleading. Marketing must not exaggerate policy coverage or suggest that all claims are guaranteed to be paid.

Advantages and limitations

Effective PR can:

Improve trust and brand credibility.
Increase awareness at a relatively low cost.
Strengthen relationships with clients and insurers.
Demonstrate Movo’s expertise.
Support client retention and referrals.

However, Movo has less control over earned media than paid advertising. Journalists, customers and social-media users may interpret a story differently from its intended message. Poorly handled complaints or inaccurate posts can also damage the company’s reputation quickly.

Relevant Knowledge, Skills and Behaviours

K1.2 – Organisation and brand

I understand that every customer email, social-media post, review response and public statement contributes to Movo’s brand. Communications should consistently reflect professionalism, expertise and customer care.

K1.3 – Stakeholder management

PR requires effective relationships with customers, insurers, underwriters, journalists, community organisations and professional networks. Each stakeholder may require a different communication style and level of technical detail.

K2.2 – Budget and resources

I understand that PR activities must be planned within an agreed budget. Movo should evaluate whether activities such as sponsorships, events and external PR support provide suitable value and contribute to measurable objectives.

S1.2 – Planning marketing activity

I can support a PR campaign by establishing SMART objectives. For example: “Publish four risk-management articles during the next three months and generate ten qualified commercial insurance enquiries.”

S1.3 – Producing marketing communications

I can draft press releases, website articles, LinkedIn posts and customer communications using clear and accurate language. I would ensure that technical insurance information is explained in a way that the target audience can understand.

S4 – Measuring performance

I can help measure PR performance through website traffic, media mentions, social-media engagement, customer enquiries, referrals, review scores and conversion rates. This would help Movo assess whether the activity achieved its objectives.

B4.1 – Integrity

I would communicate honestly and transparently, avoiding exaggerated claims about premiums, cover or claim outcomes. I would also ensure that important exclusions and limitations are not hidden or presented unfairly.

B4.3 – Professionalism

I would check communications carefully for accuracy, maintain customer confidentiality and respond appropriately to public comments. Where necessary, technical or sensitive statements would be approved by a suitable senior colleague or compliance representative.

Workplace reflection

In my role at Movo Insurance Brokers, I contribute to PR through professional communication with clients and insurers. When preparing renewal letters, recommendations or claims updates, I aim to explain information clearly and manage expectations fairly. This supports Movo’s reputation because customers judge the business not only by the insurance product offered, but also by the quality and reliability of the service they receive.

Overall, PR supports Movo’s long-term success by creating trust, demonstrating expertise and maintaining positive stakeholder relationships. In a regulated industry such as UK insurance, successful PR must always be supported by accuracy, integrity, confidentiality and professional conduct.

Reflection: Thames Water Safety Passport Training

As part of my role, I completed the Thames Water safety passport training required to access their sites. This gave me a working knowledge of the site-specific hazards, permit-to-work requirements, PPE standards, and emergency procedures that apply across their operational and construction sites, and reinforced my understanding of how health and safety legislation and CDM obligations translate into practical, on-the-ground controls (K9).

Holding this passport has directly enabled site-based project controls work. In April, I visited Harpenden to check progress against the schedule, attending site in person to verify status rather than relying solely on reported data — a practical example of using site access to support progress and schedule assurance (S9, S26). In May, I visited East Hyde to discuss value improvement opportunities with the main contractor, which meant engaging directly with a multi-disciplinary team on site to explore how efficiency could be improved on the project (B8), and reflects the kind of collaborative, in-person engagement that safety passport access makes possible. Both visits depended on valid site access being in place, which meant planning them around passport requirements and site protocols — a clear illustration of why site access has to be accounted for in project controls planning and scheduling if this kind of assurance and stakeholder engagement is to happen reliably and safely (S9).

Undertaking this training, and maintaining it for repeat visits to sites like East Hyde and Harpenden, reflects my personal commitment to a safety-first culture — not just complying with a mandatory requirement, but recognising that my own conduct on site, and my awareness of risks to others, contributes to the wider safety culture of the projects I support (B1). It also reinforces my sense of duty of care towards colleagues, contractors, and site personnel at both locations, and the importance of ensuring project controls work is carried out with that responsibility in mind (S11, K11).
Going forward, I'll continue to maintain this training and apply it whenever my role requires site visits, ensuring I remain compliant and that any progress verification, stakeholder engagement, or data validation I carry out on site — as at Harpenden and East Hyde — is done safely and in line with site protocols.

Following confirmation that the current contractor price exceeded the programme budget, I took part in a workshop convened to agree options for scope optimisation. This required applying cost engineering thinking to understand where the budget baseline had been exceeded and what scope elements could realistically be adjusted without compromising project objectives (K24). As part of the discussion, we worked through potential efficiency measures, evaluating what could be optimised against cost, time and quality to bring the solution back within budget (K23).

One of the key recommendations to emerge from the workshop was for the contractor to visit site and undertake a survey to determine whether any existing equipment could be reused rather than procured new. I contributed to shaping this recommendation, recognising its potential to materially reduce cost exposure while still meeting the technical requirements of the project (B9). Being conscious of the contractual and cost implications of the current position also meant approaching the discussion with a commercial mindset, weighing how the optimisation options would affect overall project cost and value (B3).

I helped identify and articulate the cost variance against the programme budget, explaining its potential impact and the case for pursuing scope optimisation as the recovery route, in order to support informed decision-making going forward (S26, S27). A follow-up meeting has been scheduled for May to review the outcome of the site survey and agree next steps, reflecting an adaptable approach to resolving the budget pressure as new information becomes available (B11).

We have received the clients brief but no way to prioritise and break down the work into manageable chunks.
We needed a document so that we could define each of the steps which needed to be taken to produce a successful outcome and align on scope.
This was important to ensure that internally the project stakeholders have a clear view of the steps that need to be undertaken and also so that we could be transparent with the client.
Do create this document I used a Work Break Down structure - taking the clients high level deliverables and breaking them down into subsets. Further I then scored each of the values using MOSCOW.
To create this document I ran workshop meetings with subject matter experts and will also peer review with the project assigned engineer who will be responsible for undertaking the work.

I believe that this document will have a very positive impact as it allows us to ensure that the scope is clear and expectations are aligned with all stakeholders.

 I believe that this approach will allow improved scheduling and reporting against each deliverable and ensure clear communication on progress of each deliverable.

It will also enable us to align and agree on priority items with a view to delivering early and often enabling client stakeholders to start recognising value earlier.
